chapter_summary:
Graphics are often the most visually impactful aspect of a game, but they can also be the most demanding on performance, particularly on the GPU. As a Unity Certified Programmer, you'll need to strike a balance between visual fidelity and frame rate. Rendering and graphics optimization is primarily about reducing the workload on the GPU and the CPU's rendering pipeline.

One of the most significant factors in rendering performance is the number of **draw calls**. Each time the CPU tells the GPU to draw something, it's a draw call, and each one has an associated overhead. Reducing draw calls is paramount. Unity offers several built-in mechanisms:
*   **Static Batching:** For static (non-moving) GameObjects that share the same material, Unity can combine their meshes into larger ones at build time, significantly reducing draw calls. To enable this, simply mark GameObjects as "Static" in the Inspector.
*   **Dynamic Batching:** For small, moving meshes that share the same material, Unity can combine them into a single batch at runtime. There are strict limitations on dynamic batching (e.g., vertices count, scaling, shader usage), so it's not always applicable.
*   **GPU Instancing:** This is a powerful technique for rendering many copies of the *same* mesh and material with different properties (like position, rotation, scale, color) in a single draw call. It requires shaders that support instancing and is ideal for things like trees, grass, or crowds. Standard Unity shaders often support it, and you can enable it on materials.
*   **Sprite Atlases:** For 2D games, combining multiple sprites into a single texture atlas reduces draw calls by allowing Unity to render many sprites from that atlas in one go, provided they are using the same material.

Beyond draw calls, managing scene complexity is vital. **Level of Detail (LOD)** groups allow you to define multiple versions of a mesh, each with varying levels of detail. As the camera moves further away, Unity automatically switches to lower-detail versions, reducing the number of triangles the GPU has to process. This is incredibly effective for distant objects like mountains, buildings, or large crowds. Similarly, **Occlusion Culling** is a technique that prevents Unity from rendering objects that are completely hidden by other objects (occluders) from the camera's perspective. It requires baking occlusion data in the editor (`Window > Rendering > Occlusion Culling`), but it can save significant GPU time by not drawing what the player can't see.

**Texture optimization** is another crucial area. Textures consume a large portion of GPU memory, and inefficient textures can lead to slow loading times and memory exhaustion.
*   **Compression:** Always use appropriate texture compression formats (e.g., DXT for desktop, ASTC/ETC2 for mobile). Unity provides various options in the Inspector, and choosing the right one can drastically reduce memory footprint without significant visual loss.
*   **Resolution:** Use the lowest possible resolution that still looks good. Don't use 4K textures for objects that are only seen from a distance or occupy a small portion of the screen.
*   **Mipmaps:** Enable mipmaps for 3D textures. These are pre-generated, progressively smaller versions of the texture, allowing the GPU to use a smaller, more appropriate resolution texture for distant objects, improving performance and reducing aliasing.
*   **Power of Two:** Textures with dimensions that are powers of two (e.g., 256x256, 512x1024) are often more efficient for GPU processing and compression.

**Lighting and shadows** are notoriously expensive.
*   **Light Baking (Lightmaps):** For static lights and static geometry, baking lighting information into lightmaps at edit time is far more performant than real-time lighting. Baked lights contribute zero runtime cost.
*   **Light Probes:** For dynamic objects moving through baked light environments, Light Probes capture and interpolate baked light data, allowing dynamic objects to appear correctly lit without expensive real-time calculations.
*   **Shadows:** Real-time shadows are very expensive. Reduce shadow distance, use lower shadow resolutions, and consider only casting shadows from important objects. Directional lights with hard shadows are generally cheaper than point or spot lights with soft shadows.
*   **Reflection Probes:** Similar to light probes, these capture reflections from the environment for dynamic objects, providing realistic reflections without real-time ray tracing.

Finally, **shader optimization and overdraw** are advanced topics but critical. Overdraw occurs when pixels are rendered multiple times because objects overlap. Transparent objects (particles, glass, UI) are common culprits.
*   **Shader Complexity:** Complex shaders with many calculations (e.g., multiple texture lookups, complex lighting models, extensive post-processing) take longer to execute per pixel. Use simpler shaders where possible.
*   **Alpha Clipping vs. Alpha Blending:** For objects with holes (e.g., fences, leaves), `Alpha Clipping` (discarding pixels below a certain alpha threshold) is generally cheaper and avoids overdraw compared to `Alpha Blending` (blending with what's behind), which often requires specific rendering order and can cause more overdraw.
*   **Fill Rate:** Overdraw directly impacts the GPU's fill rate. Minimize overlapping transparent geometry.

By strategically applying these techniques, you can significantly improve your game's visual performance without sacrificing too much fidelity, ensuring a smooth experience for your players.

screens.title: Rendering & Graphics Optimization
screens.subtitle: Balance visual fidelity and performance across draw calls, textures, LODs, and lighting.

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on the practical levers that control how much work the G P U and the rendering pipeline must do. You will learn what a draw call is and why reducing draw calls matters, then apply concrete techniques such as static and dynamic batching, G P U instancing, and sprite atlases to consolidate rendering work. We’ll also cover scene-level optimizations: LOD groups and occlusion culling that decide which geometry is worth drawing at a given camera location. Texture work is here too — selecting compression, mipmaps, and sensible resolutions reduces memory and load times. Finally, we examine lighting strategies like light baking and light probes and finish with shader and overdraw guidance to avoid wasted pixel work. Each topic includes a clear definition, a hands-on example, and a common misconception to avoid. By the end you’ll know which combination of techniques to try first when a scene’s frame rate drops. Think about a dense forest or a bustling city — which of these techniques would you try first to reduce G P U load?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Optimization targets the cost of drawing geometry and pixels. Reduce draw calls, simplify per-pixel work, and avoid rendering what isn’t visible.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Rendering & Graphics Optimization

Rendering & Graphics Optimization

Learn to reduce GPU and CPU load through batching, instancing, LODs, occlusion, texture work, and lighting strategies so your scenes run smoothly on target hardware.

In this lesson

Understand draw calls and practical Unity tools, then run a short lab to apply LODs, batching, and instancing to a dense forest scene.

Coming up
Draw Calls
Why each CPU-to-GPU draw costs time and how to batch them.
Lighting

Key Takeaway

Target draw calls and per-pixel work first. Use batching and instancing for geometry, atlas and compress textures for memory, and bake lighting when possible.

Concept map

How the pipeline relates

Visual overview
Draw Calls

Textures & Shaders

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus on concrete skills you can apply immediately in Unity. First, you will implement techniques to reduce draw calls using static and dynamic batching, G P U instancing, and sprite atlases. Practically, that means recognizing when to mark geometry as static, when to enable instancing on a material, and how atlases let many sprites render from one texture. Second, you will set up LOD groups and use occlusion culling so the renderer only processes what matters based on distance and visibility. That reduces both vertex and fragment work for distant or hidden objects. Third, you will choose texture compression, mipmaps, and resolutions that lower G P U memory and improve load times without obvious visual loss. Finally, you will optimize lighting through baking and probes and reduce overdraw and shader cost. For each objective you’ll see an example and a common pitfall so you can choose the right tool for the problem. Which objective is most urgent in your current project?

keyIdea.title: Focus areas
keyIdea.text: Reduce draw calls, manage scene visibility, compress textures, and bake lighting for the biggest rendering wins.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Apply & Verify
screens.subtitle: How to validate each objective in Unity projects

narration.text: Now let’s connect each objective to a verification step and a practical example. For draw calls, validate with the Profiler: measure batch counts before and after marking objects static or enabling instancing. A concrete example is a set of repeated trees; enabling G P U instancing or static batching should reduce batches. For LOD and occlusion, walk the scene and observe distant meshes switch and occluded objects disappear from rendering; the Profiler will show less vertex work. For textures, compare memory usage before and after changing compression and enabling mipmaps; inspect artifacts at different camera distances to ensure quality. For lighting and shaders, bake lightmaps and use light probes, then move a dynamic object through the scene to verify consistent lighting without runtime lights. Each verification step prevents common mistakes: assuming visual parity when memory or draw calls still indicate a problem. Which verification will you run first in your project?

screens.title: Draw Calls — What they are and why they matter
screens.subtitle: Definition, analogy, and practical impact on frame rate

narration.text: A draw call is a single command from the C P U that instructs the G P U to render a batch of geometry. Each call carries overhead: state checks, material bindings, and the command submission itself. That overhead becomes expensive when a scene issues many small draw calls per frame. A helpful analogy is a kitchen: preparing one large stew for many guests is far cheaper in overhead than cooking hundreds of separate small dishes. In Unity, reducing draw calls consolidates those small dishes into larger, more efficient operations. A concrete example: five hundred separate tree GameObjects, each with its own material, will generate dozens or hundreds of draw calls and overwhelm the C P U submission cost. A common misconception is to blame the G P U alone; often the C P U-bound draw call count causes frame drops even when the G P U could handle the triangles. Measure with the Profiler’s Rendering section and the Stats window, and then choose a batching or instancing approach based on object similarity and mobility. As you inspect a problematic scene, ask: which objects share materials and can be combined without changing behavior?

keyIdea.title: Draw calls matter
keyIdea.text: High draw call counts increase CPU overhead. Consolidate geometry and materials to reduce submissions and steady frame rate.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Draw Calls
Definition

What is a draw call?

A CPU-issued command to the GPU to render a set of geometry with a specific material and state. Each call adds submission cost regardless of triangle count.

Quick bullets
  • Every separate material or mesh can cause a new draw call.
  • CPU overhead often limits draw call scalability before the GPU is saturated.
  • Grouping similar objects reduces submissions and improves steady frame rates.
Key Takeaway

Measure draw calls first; then group and batch where it reduces CPU overhead without harming visuals.

Visual analogy & guided example
Analogy

Many small dishes = many draw calls. One combined pot = fewer calls with lower overhead.

Concrete example

500 separate trees with unique materials produce far more draw calls than the same trees using a shared material and instancing or batching.

Common misconception

It’s easy to assume the GPU is the only bottleneck. Often the CPU’s draw call submission is the limiting factor — measure both sides before optimizing.

Try this
Open the Stats window and record draw calls before changes.
Check
Group meshes by material and re-measure.
Reflect
Which objects are candidates for batching or instancing?

screens.title: Static & Dynamic Batching
screens.subtitle: When to use each and how Unity combines meshes

narration.text: Batching reduces draw calls by combining meshes and materials so fewer submissions are required. Static batching targets non-moving GameObjects that share a material; Unity merges their meshes at build time, creating larger combined geometry and dramatically lowering draw calls for purely static scenes. To use static batching, mark objects as static in the Inspector and ensure materials match. Dynamic batching attempts the same idea at runtime for small moving meshes but comes with strict limits: vertex counts must be low, and certain shader features or per-object scale can disable it. That means dynamic batching is great for small props, but not for large skinned characters or scaled meshes. A common pitfall is assuming dynamic batching works everywhere; if you see it not triggering, check vertex count and shader compatibility. A practical workflow is: mark true static geometry for static batching, reserve dynamic batching for tiny objects, and fall back to G P U instancing for many moving copies of the same mesh. Which objects in your scene are truly static and safe to mark? Static & Dynamic Batching means mark truly static objects for static batching. use dynamic batching only for small moving meshes with compatible shaders.. In practical terms, when to use each and how unity combines meshes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Batch selection
keyIdea.text: Mark truly static objects for static batching. Use dynamic batching only for small moving meshes with compatible shaders.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Static & Dynamic Batching
How static batching works

Static batching

Combine non-moving GameObjects sharing the same material into large meshes at build time. This reduces per-frame draw calls for static geometry with zero runtime merge cost.

Steps
  1. Mark GameObjects as Static in the Inspector.
  2. Ensure shared materials across objects.
  3. Bake lighting and generate to finalize build-time combining.
Common mistake: marking many objects static without checking light bake or load-time impact.
Dynamic batching

When dynamic batching applies

Unity can combine many small moving meshes at runtime if they meet vertex and shader restrictions. It’s automatic when conditions are met but has strict limits on vertex count and shader variants.

Good for

Small props like bullets, small debris, or simple enemies.

Bad for

Skinned meshes, large vertex-count objects, or complex shaders.

Try
Group small dynamic props under a shared material.
Pitfall
Assuming dynamic batching removes the need for instancing for many moving copies.

screens.title: GPU Instancing
screens.subtitle: Render many identical meshes efficiently with per-instance variation

narration.text: G P U instancing lets the G P U draw many copies of the same mesh and material in a single draw call while supplying per-instance properties like transform or color. This is ideal when many objects are visually identical but positioned differently, such as grass blades, trees of the same model, or repeated props. To use instancing, shaders must support it and the material must have instancing enabled. A concrete example is a field of identical rocks: with instancing each rock can have a different position and tint but still be rendered in one or a few draw calls. A common misconception is to enable instancing for every repeated object; instancing helps when the mesh and material are identical, but if you have many unique materials or high per-instance variation that requires separate shader state, instancing benefits shrink. Also remember static batching and instancing are complementary: static batching is better for truly static geometry while instancing fits many moving identical objects. After enabling instancing, always re-measure batch counts to confirm the expected reduction. GPU Instancing means use gpu instancing for many identical meshes with per-instance transforms; enable it on materials whose shaders support instancing.. In practical terms, render many identical meshes efficiently with per-instance variation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: When to instance
keyIdea.text: Use GPU instancing for many identical meshes with per-instance transforms; enable it on materials whose shaders support instancing.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › GPU Instancing
Definition

What instancing does

Instancing issues a single draw command to render many copies of the same mesh while supplying per-instance data. It minimizes CPU-to-GPU overhead for repeated geometry.

Concrete example

A field of identical grass blades can render with dramatically fewer draw calls when instanced, while each blade still gets its own position and slight color variation.

Misconception: Instancing always wins. It only helps when meshes and materials are the same and shader supports instancing.
How to enable
  • Use a shader that supports GPU instancing (many Standard/URP/HDRP shaders do).
  • On the material inspector, check "Enable GPU Instancing."
  • Provide per-instance data where needed, such as color or transform matrices.
Good fit

Many moving copies with identical material.

Not fit

Unique materials or heavy per-instance shader variants.

Check
After enabling instancing, observe batch counts in the Profiler to confirm fewer draw calls.

screens.title: Sprite Atlases & 2D Batching
screens.subtitle: Reduce draw calls for 2D games using atlases and shared materials

narration.text: In 2D games, draw calls often balloon because each sprite may use its own texture and material. A sprite atlas combines many smaller sprites into a single larger texture so the G P U can sample many images from one texture and one material. When sprites share the same atlas and material, Unity can batch them together and render many sprites with a single draw call. A real example: a UI with dozens of small icons or a group of characters built from multiple small parts. Packing those parts into an atlas eliminates material switches and reduces batches. A common mistake is packing everything into one giant atlas without considering platform memory or mipmap behavior; very large atlases can cause wasted memory or inefficient compression. Use atlases for frequently batched sprites and keep an eye on texture compression settings per platform. Which sprite sets in your project could be grouped into an atlas for immediate savings? Sprite Atlases & 2D Batching means use sprite atlases so multiple sprites share a texture and material, enabling the renderer to batch them into fewer draw calls.. In practical terms, reduce draw calls for 2d games using atlases and shared materials. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: 2D batching rule
keyIdea.text: Use sprite atlases so multiple sprites share a texture and material, enabling the renderer to batch them into fewer draw calls.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Sprite Atlases
Problem

Many sprite draw calls

Multiple sprites using separate textures lead to material switches and many draw calls. Atlases reduce those material swaps.

Concrete example

A UI composed of dozens of icons from one atlas can render with a single material and far fewer draw calls compared to separate textures for each icon.

Pitfall: Oversized atlases may be inefficient to compress on some platforms; balance packing with platform constraints.
How to approach
  • Group sprites that render together into the same atlas.
  • Ensure the sprites use the same material so batching can occur.
  • Test on target platforms to confirm compression and memory are acceptable.
Good

UI icons and frequently co-rendered sprites.

Avoid

Packing rarely used sprites into the same atlas as high-frequency ones without need.

Check
Use the Sprite Atlas system and test draw call counts in the Profiler.

screens.title: Level of Detail (LOD) Groups
screens.subtitle: Reduce polycount for distant objects with smooth transitions

narration.text: Level of Detail, or LOD, uses multiple mesh versions of an object at decreasing detail so the G P U sees fewer triangles for distant objects. In practice you create LOD 0 with full detail, then LOD 1 and LOD 2 with simplified meshes or billboards. Unity switches between them based on camera distance and screen relative size. This is especially effective for repeated distant geometry like buildings, crowds, or trees. A hands-on example is replacing the furthest LOD of a tree with a billboard sprite to cut geometry dramatically. A common mistake is using LODs only for a few objects; LODs pay off most when many instances of the same model appear at distance. When setting transition percentages, watch for popping — you can tune crossfade or use screen-relative settings to smooth transitions. After applying LODs, profile to confirm G P U triangle throughput drops and the visual trade-off is acceptable. Which repeated models in your scene should get LODs first? Level of Detail (LOD) Groups means swap to simpler meshes as camera distance increases to reduce triangle processing without significant visual loss.. In practical terms, reduce polycount for distant objects with smooth transitions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: LOD principle
keyIdea.text: Swap to simpler meshes as camera distance increases to reduce triangle processing without significant visual loss.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › LOD Groups
Definition

LOD groups explained

Provide reduced-detail meshes for the same object so Unity can render lower-polygon versions automatically as distance increases.

Steps to implement
  1. Add an LOD Group component to the prefab.
  2. Assign high-, medium-, and low-detail meshes to LOD 0, LOD 1, LOD 2 slots.
  3. Adjust transition percentages and test in Play mode.
Example & tuning

For a forest, use high-detail trees for nearby camera positions, medium for mid-distance, and billboard or very low-poly meshes for far-away trees to reduce both CPU and GPU work.

Good fit

Repeated models seen at multiple distances.

Watch for

Visible popping; use crossfade or adjust thresholds.

Check
Confirm triangle count reduction in the Profiler and acceptability of visual changes at each LOD level.

screens.title: Occlusion Culling
screens.subtitle: Baking visibility so hidden objects aren’t rendered

narration.text: Occlusion culling prevents Unity from rendering objects that are completely hidden from the camera by other geometry. Instead of drawing and then discarding pixels, occlusion culling uses precomputed visibility data to skip objects entirely. You bake occlusion data in the editor through Window → Rendering → Occlusion Culling. The workflow is: mark occluders and occludees in the scene, configure bake settings for cell size and accuracy, and run the bake. A practical demonstration is a building interior where walls occlude many objects in adjacent rooms; occlusion culling removes those hidden objects, lowering draw calls and fragment work. A common misconception is expecting occlusion culling to handle partially visible objects — it only culls objects completely hidden from the camera. Also, dynamic objects require careful setup or custom culling logic. After baking, profile to confirm fewer rendered objects and a steadier frame rate. Where in your scene do large occluders hide many other objects? Occlusion Culling means bake visibility so the renderer skips objects fully hidden by geometry, saving draw calls and fragment work.. In practical terms, baking visibility so hidden objects aren’t rendered. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Occlusion purpose
keyIdea.text: Bake visibility so the renderer skips objects fully hidden by geometry, saving draw calls and fragment work.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Occlusion Culling
What it does

Skip hidden objects

Occlusion culling precomputes which objects are visible from different parts of the scene so Unity doesn’t render objects fully hidden behind occluders.

Bake steps
  1. Open Occlusion Culling window and mark occluders/occludees.
  2. Adjust cell size and smallest occluder settings.
  3. Run Bake and test in Play mode while surveying hidden object counts.
Practical impact

In a crowded urban scene, large building facades occlude distant streets. With occlusion culling baked, those distant objects aren’t submitted to the GPU, saving both CPU and GPU time.

Good to know

Only fully hidden objects are culled; partial visibility still renders normally.

Dynamic objects

Dynamic objects may need scripts or disabled/ enabled flags to interact with baked occlusion correctly.

Check
After baking, observe the Renderer counts in the Profiler and ensure previously hidden objects no longer appear in the rendered set.

screens.title: Texture Optimization
screens.subtitle: Compression, resolution, mipmaps, and power-of-two sizing

narration.text: Textures often dominate G P U memory. Optimizing them reduces load times and memory pressure. Compression uses platform-appropriate formats — for example, pick a compressed format suited to your target hardware — to shrink texture size with minimal visible loss. Resolution matters: use the lowest resolution that still looks acceptable; distant objects do not need 4K textures. Mipmaps generate smaller prefiltered versions for distant sampling and reduce aliasing while saving bandwidth for smaller screen-space footprints. Power-of-two dimensions are generally more efficient for compression and G P U processing. A concrete example is converting a 2048x2048 distant rock texture to 512x512 with mipmaps and a compressed format; memory drops significantly while the rock looks fine in distance. A common pitfall is overcompressing textures and introducing artifacts; always test on target hardware. After changes, monitor G P U memory and loading behavior to confirm improvements. Which large textures in your project are good candidates for downscaling and compression? Texture Optimization means right-size textures, enable mipmaps for 3d assets, and choose compression formats appropriate to the target platform.. In practical terms, compression, resolution, mipmaps, and power-of-two sizing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Texture triage
keyIdea.text: Right-size textures, enable mipmaps for 3D assets, and choose compression formats appropriate to the target platform.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Texture Optimization
Key techniques
  • Compression: choose formats that target your platform to lower GPU memory.
  • Resolution: reduce textures that aren’t seen close-up.
  • Mipmaps: enable for 3D textures to reduce aliasing and bandwidth at distance.
  • Power-of-two: prefer sizes like 256, 512, 1024 for efficient compression.
Example
Change a distant environment texture from 2048 to 512, enable mipmaps, and set platform compression to reduce memory and maintain visual quality at distance.
Checklist
Measure

Check GPU memory usage before and after changes.

Visual test

Inspect textures at multiple distances to spot artifacts.

Pitfall
Don’t overcompress critical close-up textures; balance memory and fidelity per asset use.

screens.title: Lighting, Lightmaps, and Light Probes
screens.subtitle: Move expensive lighting work offline and use probes for dynamics

narration.text: Lighting and shadows are expensive if computed in real time. Light baking moves static lighting calculations into textures called lightmaps so static geometry doesn’t cost runtime lighting. Bake static lights for architecture and environmental illumination to eliminate many per-frame calculations. For dynamic objects that move through a baked environment, use light probes: these capture the baked lighting at probe samples and interpolate lighting for dynamic renderers, giving plausible shading without runtime light costs. Shadows are costly as well; reduce shadow distance and lower shadow resolution, and limit shadow casters to the most important objects. Reflection probes capture environmental reflections for dynamic objects without real-time ray tracing. A practical example is baking a city block’s street lights into lightmaps, placing probes for moving cars, and limiting real-time shadow casters to major dynamic actors. A common misconception is that baked lighting eliminates all visual realism; probes and well-configured lightmaps retain much of the visual quality with far less runtime cost. How can you partition your scene into static and dynamic elements for efficient lighting? Lighting, Lightmaps, and Light Probes means bake static lighting into lightmaps and use light probes and reflection probes for dynamic objects to cut runtime cost while preserving realistic lighting.. In practical terms, move expensive lighting work offline and use probes for dynamics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lighting trade-off
keyIdea.text: Bake static lighting into lightmaps and use light probes and reflection probes for dynamic objects to cut runtime cost while preserving realistic lighting.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Lighting & Shadows
Core idea

Bake static light, probe dynamic light

Use lightmaps for static geometry to eliminate real-time lighting cost. Use light probes and reflection probes to give dynamic objects plausible lighting and reflections without per-frame expensive calculations.

Concrete example

Bake all static buildings and street fixtures. Place light probes along paths where players and NPCs move so they receive interpolated baked lighting during gameplay.

Performance tips
  • Reduce shadow distance and resolution for less GPU cost.
  • Limit real-time shadow casters to key moving objects.
  • Use reflection probes for static reflection capture where possible.
Pitfall
Failing to mark objects static prevents them from benefiting from light baking and wastes runtime resources.

screens.title: Shader Complexity & Overdraw
screens.subtitle: Reduce per-pixel cost and avoid redundant pixel rendering

narration.text: Shader complexity and overdraw are advanced but frequently decisive performance factors. Shader complexity refers to how many operations a shader performs per pixel — multiple texture lookups, complex lighting math, and many branches all increase per-pixel cost. Overdraw occurs when the same screen pixel is shaded multiple times because geometry overlaps, which is common with many transparent objects. Transparent materials typically force a specific render order and can cause heavy overdraw. A common optimization is to prefer alpha clipping for objects with holes, such as fences or leaves, because clipping discards pixels outright and avoids blending-based overdraw. Another approach is to simplify shaders: reduce texture lookups, precompute lighting where possible, and minimize expensive functions. To evaluate, profile fragment cost and use the Scene view’s overdraw visualization. The practical example: replace alpha-blended vegetation with alpha-clipped cards and lower the shader’s instruction count to reduce fill-rate pressure. After these changes, re-profile to confirm lower G P U fragment time. Which transparent materials in your scene cause the most overdraw? Shader Complexity & Overdraw means simplify shaders and minimize overdraw, especially with transparent geometry; prefer clipping over blending where it reduces redundant pixel work.. In practical terms, reduce per-pixel cost and avoid redundant pixel rendering. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pixel economy
keyIdea.text: Simplify shaders and minimize overdraw, especially with transparent geometry; prefer clipping over blending where it reduces redundant pixel work.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Shader & Overdraw
Shader cost

Keep shaders lean

Reduce texture samples and complex lighting math in shaders. Where possible, precompute data or use cheaper approximations to lower per-pixel execution time.

Small wins
  • Remove unnecessary branches and expensive functions.
  • Use simpler lighting models for distant or less-important objects.
Overdraw

Avoid redundant pixel shading

Overdraw happens when pixels are drawn multiple times due to overlapping geometry and transparency. Prefer alpha clipping to avoid blending where it reduces redundant rendering.

Example

Swap blended foliage to clipped cards to reduce fill rate and avoid heavy overdraw.

Measure

Use overdraw visualization and fragment profiling to find hotspots.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Core terms to keep in mind

narration.text: These core terms are practical anchors as you profile and optimize. A draw call is the C P U’s command to render geometry — reducing these is often the first optimization. Static batching merges non-moving objects that share materials at build time, while dynamic batching does similar work at runtime but only for small compatible meshes. G P U instancing renders many identical meshes in a single draw call with different per-instance data, ideal for repeated moving objects. Sprite atlases combine many 2D images into one texture so the renderer can batch sprites together. Keep these terms in mind when you inspect the Profiler; each leads you to a concrete tool in Unity. How might these terms change your approach the next time you open a heavy scene? Static Batching
Combine static meshes with the same material at build time to lower draw calls.
GPU Instancing
Render many identical meshes in one draw call with per-instance data like transform or tint.
Summary

Use these concepts as first checks when a scene’s render performance drops: measure, group, and re-measure.

narration.text: Texture compression, mipmaps, and power-of-two sizing reduce memory and bandwidth pressure. Light baking and light probes move expensive lighting work offline while preserving dynamic object lighting quality. Occlusion culling prevents completely hidden objects from being rendered at all, saving both C P U and G P U work. Finally, watch for shader complexity and overdraw: simplify shader math and prefer alpha clipping for cutouts to avoid redundant pixel shading. Each of these ideas directly maps to measurable improvements — lower memory use, fewer rendered triangles, and less fragment time.
